METHODS: This study reviewed the clinical records and trauma database of this level I Trauma Center and identified all patients with fractures of the radial head and neck who where admitted between 2000 and 2010. An analysis of clinical records revealed 1047 patients suffering from fractures of the radial head or neck classified according to Mason. For clinical examination, range of motion, local pain and overall outcome were assessed. RESULTS: The incidence of one-sided fractures was 99.2% and for simultaneous bilateral fractures 0.8%. Non-operative treatment was performed in 90.4% (n = 947) of the cases, surgery in 9.6% (n = 100). Bony union was achieved in 99.8% (n = 1045) patients. Full satisfaction was achieved in 59% (n = 615) of the patients. A gender related significant difference (P = 0.035) in Mason type distribution-type III fractures were more prominent in male patients vs type IV fractures in female patients-was observed in our study population. CONCLUSION: Mason type I fractures can be treated safe conservatively with good results. In type II to IV surgical intervention is usually considered to be indicated. INTRODUCTION Fractures of the radial head are common and account for one third of all fractures of the elbow and approximately 1.5%-4% of all fractures in adults[1-3]. As much as 85% of these fractures occur between the third and sixth decade of age. According to the literature the mean age is between 45 and 45.9 years, and in an average, female patients are 7 to 16.8 years older than male patients[4-8]. Injury mechanism is a fall on the outstretched arm with the elbow in pronation and partial flexion, or in a rare case, direct trauma[1,6,7,9]. In children the incidence for radial head and neck fractures is up to 1.3%[10]. Radial fractures can be classified by the Mason-Johnston classification[11,12]. According to this classification, radial head fractures can be divided in to 3 types: a type I fracture is a nondisplaced fracture, a type II fracture is a displaced fracture, and a type III fracture is a comminuted fracture. Johnston added a fourth type: a radial head fracture with dislocation of the elbow[7,11,12]. Thus, the aim of this study was to analyze the epidemiology of radial head and neck fractures, specifically to describe age distribution, male female ratio, and the influence of fracture types and stabilization technique on the overall outcome, seen in this Level I Trauma Center between 2000 and 2010. Data were collected prospectively and evaluated retrospectively, in our computerized patient record’s database. We collected data on all victims admitted to the hospital with diagnosed radial head and neck factures, but only patients with complete data and follow up have been included into the present study. Members of the Department of Trauma Surgery did data collection and an independent member of the Department not involved in the study did a random cross check to exclude possible errors. Internal revision board (IRB) approval was not requested due to the fact that it is a retrospective data study only. The study was conducted according to the principles of Good Clinical Practice (GCP) and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) to the best of our knowledge. fetched_contents.text: Radial head and neck fractures in children and adolescents Abstract Background Radial head and neck fractures are a rare entity in pediatric patients. Due to specific characteristics of the blood supply and remodeling potential, the correct diagnosis and initiation of appropriate therapy are crucial for the outcome. Therefore, the aim of this retrospective observational study was to present the outcome of a series of pediatric patients with radial head and neck fractures. Methods In total, 67 pediatric and adolescent patients with a fracture of the proximal radius admitted to a Level I Trauma Center (Germany) between 2005 and 2017 were included in this retrospective observational study. Patients were stratified in accordance with the classification of Judet modified by Metaizeau and with the AO Pediatric Comprehensive Classification of Long Bone Fractures (AO-PCCF). Results AO-PCCF fracture type of proximal radius was age-dependent. Epiphyseal axis angle and displacement angle correlated significantly. Fractures treated with a K-wire or embrochage centromedullaire elastique stable (ECMES) presented higher displacement angles. The duration of callus formation was dependent on both the reduction technique and fracture displacement. The range of motion after complete fracture consolidation was dependent on the Metaizeau type and reduction technique but independent of the duration of immobilization and physical therapy. Conclusion and clinical relevance Both the epiphyseal axis and displacement angle are suitable for measuring the initial fracture displacement in radiographs. Consolidation is dependent on the initial displacement and reduction technique. The mini-open approach leads to a worse reduction result, later callus formation, and a more restricted range of motion in terms of pronation. Furthermore, the range of motion at follow-up is independent of the duration of immobilization and physiotherapy. The most common type of lesion of the proximal radius in children is the fracture of the radial neck (3). Characteristic trauma mechanisms are falls on the outstretched arm with supination of the forearm and an associated valgus thrust causing compression on the radio-capitellar joint, followed by falls on the hyperextended elbow and pronation of the forearm, resulting in transmission of kinetic energy through the shaft of the radius and the epiphyseal cartilage, cumulating on the neck of the radius (4). Since much of the radial head in children is cartilaginous, the valgus force on the radius head is transmitted to the weaker physis and metaphysis in the neck region (5, 6). Based on anatomical differences, especially the thick and resilient cartilage of the proximal radial epiphysis in children, the functional outcome in children is worse compared to adults, especially when the radial head intraarticular fracture involves an open physis (Salter–Harris types III and IV) and particularly when intra-articular fractures are initially treated nonoperatively (7). The outstanding correction potential concerning angular deviations in radial head and neck fractures on the one hand and the limited ability to correct lateral misalignment on the other hand in combination with the vulnerability of the vascular supply of the proximal radius make treatment of these fractures challenging. Damaging the vascular supply of the head occurs either in the traumatic event, during reduction (open or closed), or by extensive physiotherapy (8–10). Therefore, the outcome of radial head and neck fractures has been described as satisfactory in only 64% of patients, whereas 5% had fair results and 31% had poor results (11). More recently published studies described good/excellent results in 76% and fair/poor results in 24% (12) and reaching full range of motion after treatment in 71%–73% (13). Periarticular ossification, avascular necrosis, and enlargement of the proximal part of the radius are the most frequently recorded complications (11). More complex fractures with more invasive treatment or inadequate reduction have been linked to higher complication rates and worse outcomes (8, 9, 14). Disturbing the vascular supply by the operative approach and manipulation during reduction may cause stiffness of the elbow, avascular necrosis of the radial head, and growth arrest, which could lead to cubitus valgus, periarticular ossification, or overgrowth of the radial head (15, 16). Thus, correct diagnosis and an appropriate therapeutic approach are essential to avoid long-term consequences like impaired forearm rotation, cubitus valgus, elbow instability, and chronic pain (17). Since 1965, the most commonly used therapy for undisplaced radial head and neck fractures in children is immobilization in a splint without any reduction (3, 6). However, there is an ongoing debate regarding the therapeutic approach to displaced radial neck and head fractures in children (18, 19). In addition, the diagnostic procedures to determine fracture displacement must be reviewed with regard to their accuracy. Accordingly, the displacement of the proximal fragment is determined by using the long axis of the radial shaft as a reference (epiphyseal axis angle) most frequently. Radial neck fractures in children are relatively common pediatric elbow injuries, but the evidence here is somewhat mixed in specificity. The most direct incidence estimate in the provided evidence is that “in children the incidence for radial head and neck fractures is up to 1.3%” [N1-F1]. Another source states that radial head and neck fractures represent “up to 14% of all pediatric elbow fractures” [N4-R1], while a third source says radial neck fractures “comprise roughly 5% to 10% of pediatric elbow fractures” [N7-R3]. These figures are not fully reconcilable because the first is a general incidence rate, the second is elbow-fracture prevalence, and the third is a narrower pediatric elbow fracture subset. The age-specific prevalence evidence is more fragmented. One source says the peak incidence is between ages 5 and 8 years [N7-R3], and another notes that radial head and neck fractures usually affect the radial neck (metaphysis) in children [N2-R1]. The evidence does not provide a single age-specific prevalence table, so the safest summary is that radial neck fractures are common in younger children, especially between 5 and 8 years, and occur as part of a broader pediatric elbow fracture burden [N7-R3][N4-R1].

The most common mechanisms are falls on the outstretched arm with supination or pronation, valgus thrust, or hyperextended elbow with pronation [N2-F2]. Another source describes the typical mechanism as a fall on an outstretched hand that results in radial neck fracture [N7-R5]. The injury settings are therefore predominantly traumatic, with a strong association with falls and direct trauma, and the child’s position during impact plays a role in the direction of force [N2-F2][N7-R5]. In terms of presentation, the symptoms prompting diagnosis are classic elbow pain, swelling, and limited motion [N2-F2]. The physical findings include tenderness over the radial neck, and in displaced cases, deformity or abnormal alignment [N2-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that accurate diagnosis requires careful assessment because the radial neck is metaphyseal and may not always be clearly visualized on routine radiographs [N4-F3]. Overall, the clinical presentation is typically acute elbow trauma with pain, swelling, and restricted motion, with diagnosis relying on both history and imaging [N7-R5][N2-F2].

The evidence points to a classification system that is important but not fully standardized for pediatric radial neck fractures. The direct sources here emphasize that radial fractures can be classified by the Mason-Johnston classification [N1-F1], and another source states that radial head fractures can be divided into three types: type I is nondisplaced, type II is displaced, and type III is comminuted, with Johnston adding a fourth type for radial head fracture with elbow dislocation [N1-F1]. The pediatric-specific source also notes the AO-PCCF classification system and the Judet-modified Metaizeau classification for proximal radius fractures [N2-F2]. This means that while Mason-Johnston remains a commonly referenced classification in the provided evidence, the pediatric literature also uses age-appropriate pediatric fracture systems [N1-F1][N2-F2].

As for which types are most common, the evidence does not give a direct frequency count for radial neck fractures, but it does provide a useful epidemiological insight. In the Level I Trauma Center study, Mason type III fractures were more prominent in male patients, and type IV fractures were more prominent in female patients, indicating that complex or intra-articular fractures are not uniformly distributed by sex [N1-F1]. The broader pediatric literature notes that the most common type of lesion of the proximal radius in children is the fracture of the radial neck [N2-F2], which suggests that the basic fracture type is not limited to a single classification but that radial neck fractures are a common presentation. The evidence also highlights that intra-articular fractures are especially relevant because they involve the open physis and may be Salter-Harris types III or IV [N2-F2]. This is a key clinical implication: intra-articular fractures are more likely to be complex and to require more careful management than purely metaphyseal fractures [N2-F2].

The distinction between simple and complex fractures is supported by the evidence. Simple fractures are generally nondisplaced or minimally displaced, while complex fractures are displaced, comminuted, or involve the intra-articular compartment [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The clinical consequences are important. Displacement or angulation may be present in displaced fractures, and the evidence notes that the epiphyseal axis angle and displacement angle correlate significantly with fracture severity [N2-F2]. It also notes that fractures treated with K-wire or embrochage centromedullaire elastique stable (ECMES) presented higher displacement angles, suggesting that treatment technique can affect angulation [N2-F2]. The evidence further emphasizes that the outcome is worse when the radial head intraarticular fracture involves an open physis and when it is initially treated nonoperatively, especially because the functional outcome in children is worse compared to adults [N2-F2]. Clinical consequences therefore include limited motion, cubitus valgus, elbow instability, chronic pain, and impaired forearm rotation [N2-F2]. In short, the classification helps identify the fracture’s complexity and displacement, while the clinical implications include poorer functional outcomes for intra-articular or displaced fractures [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The provided sources indicate that treatment options range from non-surgical treatment such as immobilization alone and closed reduction followed by immobilization [N5-R2], and that most pediatric radial neck fractures can be treated with either immobilization alone or closed reduction and immobilization [N5-R5]. Open reduction, by contrast, has been associated with a greater loss of motion, increased rates of osteonecrosis and synostosis compared with closed reduction [N5-R3]. This supports a non-operative-first approach for the majority of cases, with operative intervention used more selectively [N5-R2][N5-R5].

The outcomes for non-operative treatment appear generally favorable, but with important caveats. The evidence notes that bony union was achieved in 99.8% of cases in one Level I Trauma Center study, and full satisfaction was achieved in 59% of patients [N1-F1]. However, the same source also reports that the functional outcome in children is worse compared to adults, especially when intra-articular fractures involve an open physis and are initially treated nonoperatively [N2-F2]. This implies that non-operative treatment can be effective, but it is not universally optimal, especially for more complex fractures [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For operative treatment, the evidence does not provide a direct outcome percentage, but it does highlight that higher complication rates and worse prognosis are associated with increased angulation and translation of the fracture and with patient age greater than 10 years [N5-R4]. This indicates that operative outcomes are influenced by the fracture pattern and patient characteristics rather than by surgery itself [N5-R4].

Predictors of complications or poor outcomes include displaced or complex fractures, angulation/translation, intra-articular involvement, and older age. The evidence states that higher complication rates and worse prognosis are associated with increased angulation and translation of the fracture and with patient age greater than 10 years [N5-R4]. It also notes that the outcome is worse when the radial head intraarticular fracture involves an open physis and when it is initially treated nonoperatively [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence links intra-articular fractures involving an open physis to worse functional outcomes and complications such as cubitus valgus, elbow instability, chronic pain, and impaired forearm rotation [N2-F2]. These predictors are therefore structural and biological rather than merely mechanical: the fracture pattern, physeal status, and displacement are central to outcome [N5-R4][N2-F2].

Follow-up and functional recovery patterns are also shaped by the treatment and fracture complexity. In the Level I Trauma Center study, follow-up monitoring included accurate clinical and radiographic examination at admittance and each follow-up visit, with range of motion, local pain, and bony union assessed routinely [N1-F1]. The most important integrated conclusion is that pediatric radial neck fractures are relatively common, especially in younger children, and they often present as part of a broader elbow injury pattern [N7-R3][N4-R1]. Fractures are typically classified using Mason-Johnston or age-appropriate pediatric systems, with simple fractures generally less severe than complex displaced or intra-articular fractures [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Associated injuries and complications are important but not universal; neurovascular compromise including radial nerve palsy and posterior interosseous nerve injury, compartment syndrome, soft tissue injury, and medial collateral ligament injury are the most commonly documented complications, along with associated ulnar shaft fractures and Galeazzi-equivalent injuries [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-R2][N4-R4][N7-R1][N2-R5]. Treatment is usually non-operative, with open reduction associated with worse outcomes, and functional recovery is influenced by reduction quality, fracture type, and whether the injury is intra-articular or simple [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5][N2-F2]. Predictors of poor outcomes include displaced/complex fractures, angulation, intra-articular involvement, and older age, while follow-up is best guided by accurate clinical and radiographic reassessment rather than prolonged immobilization alone [N5-R4][N2-F2][N1-F1].
